claim: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant mRNA modification.
source: N6-methyladenosine (m6A), the most abundant mRNA modification, is deposited in mammals/insects/plants by m6A methyltransferase complexes (MTC) comprising a catalytic subunit and at least five additional proteins.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental support in this manuscript.

claim: m6A is deposited in mammals/insects/plants by m6A methyltransferase complexes (MTC) comprising a catalytic subunit and at least five additional proteins.
source: N6-methyladenosine (m6A), the most abundant mRNA modification, is deposited in mammals/insects/plants by m6A methyltransferase complexes (MTC) comprising a catalytic subunit and at least five additional proteins.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about MTC composition across species.

claim: The yeast MTC was previously known to comprise three proteins, of which two were conserved.
source: The yeast MTC is critical for meiosis and was known to comprise three proteins, of which two were conserved.
evidence: This refers to prior knowledge about yeast MTC composition before this study.

claim: The yeast MTC comprises three novel components: Kar4, Ygl036w (Vir1), and Dyn2.
source: We uncover three novel MTC components (Kar4/Ygl036w-Vir1/Dyn2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by IP-MS experiments shown in Figures 1B, 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: All MTC subunits except for Dyn2 are essential for m6A deposition.
source: All MTC subunits, except for Dyn2, are essential for m6A deposition and have corresponding mammalian MTC orthologues.
evidence: This is supported by m6A quantification experiments shown in Figures 1D-F and Figure 2.

claim: All MTC subunits except for Dyn2 have corresponding mammalian MTC orthologues.
source: All MTC subunits, except for Dyn2, are essential for m6A deposition and have corresponding mammalian MTC orthologues.
evidence: This is supported by sequence and structural alignment analyses shown in Figure 3.

claim: The yeast MTC is unipartite, unlike the mammalian bipartite MTC.
source: Unlike the mammalian bipartite MTC, the yeast MTC is unipartite, yet multifunctional.
evidence: This is inferred from protein interaction and stability data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The mRNA interacting module comprises Ime4, Mum2, Vir1, and Kar4.
source: The mRNA interacting module, comprising Ime4, Mum2, Vir1, and Kar4, exerts the MTC's m6A-independent function, while Slz1 enables the MTC catalytic function in m6A deposition.
evidence: This is supported by protein interaction data (Figure 4) and RNA binding assays (Figure 6).

claim: Slz1 enables the MTC catalytic function in m6A deposition.
source: The mRNA interacting module, comprising Ime4, Mum2, Vir1, and Kar4, exerts the MTC's m6A-independent function, while Slz1 enables the MTC catalytic function in m6A deposition.
evidence: This is supported by m6A quantification in slz1Δ cells (Figures 1D-E) and phenotypic analysis (Figure 5).

claim: Both m6A-dependent and m6A-independent functions of the MTC are critical for meiotic progression.
source: Both functions are critical for meiotic progression.
evidence: This is supported by meiotic progression assays and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Kar4 has a mechanistically separate role from the MTC during mating.
source: Kar4 also has a mechanistically separate role from the MTC during mating.
evidence: This is supported by protein expression, localization, and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6.

claim: m6A is the most widespread internal RNA modification on mammalian messenger RNA (mRNAs).
source: The N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification is the most widespread internal RNA modification on mammalian messenger RNA (mRNAs).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The catalytic subunit of the MTC is METTL3 in human and Ime4 in yeast.
source: The mark is deposited by a multi-subunit protein complex, also known as the m6A methyltransferase ('writer') complex (MTC), of which the catalytic subunit is METTL3 in human and Ime4 in yeast (Balacco and Soller, 2019; Clancy et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In mammals, m6A deposition occurs at DRACH motifs throughout transcripts that are distant from splice sites.
source: In mammals, the deposition of m6A occurs at DRACH motifs throughout transcripts that are distant from splice sites, biasing this modification towards long internal and last exons (Dominissini et al., 2012; Meyer et al., 2012; Uzonyi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: m6A modification is biased towards long internal and last exons in mammals.
source: In mammals, the deposition of m6A occurs at DRACH motifs throughout transcripts that are distant from splice sites, biasing this modification towards long internal and last exons (Dominissini et al., 2012; Meyer et al., 2012; Uzonyi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The presence of m6A on mRNA primarily impacts mRNA stability.
source: The presence of m6A on mRNA primarily impacts mRNA stability but has also been linked to a wide array of additional molecular outcomes, and its disruption is associated with diverse phenotypes ranging from immune dysfunction to cancer (Jiang et al., 2021; Murakami and Jaffrey, 2022; Zaccara et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Disruption of m6A is associated with diverse phenotypes ranging from immune dysfunction to cancer.
source: The presence of m6A on mRNA primarily impacts mRNA stability but has also been linked to a wide array of additional molecular outcomes, and its disruption is associated with diverse phenotypes ranging from immune dysfunction to cancer (Jiang et al., 2021; Murakami and Jaffrey, 2022; Zaccara et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: METTL3 forms a hetero dimer complex with METTL14, which is the catalytic unit of the MTC.
source: METTL3, which forms a hetero dimer complex with METTL14, is the catalytic unit of the MTC (Liu et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Several auxiliary proteins that interact with METTL3/METTL14 are required for the deposition of m6A, including WTAP, VIRMA, HAKAI, ZCH13H3, and RBM15/RBM15b.
source: Several auxiliary proteins that interact with METTL3/METTL14 are required for the deposition of m6A. These include the scaffold proteins WTAP and VIRMA, E3 ligase HAKAI, ZCH13H3, and RNA binding proteins RBM15/RBM15b (Bawankar et al., 2021; Knuckles et al., 2018; Ping et al., 2014; Schwartz et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2021; Wen et al., 2018; Yue et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mammalian and Drosophila MTCs can be divided into two subcomplexes: MAC (consisting of METTL3/METTL14) and MACOM (consisting of WTAP, VIRMA, HAKAI, ZCH13H3, and RBM15/RBM15b).
source: Structural and topological analyses of the mammalian and Drosophila MTCs revealed that MTCs can be divided into two subcomplexes: (1) the m6A METTL complex (MAC) which consists of METTL3/METTL14, and an (2) m6A-METTL-associated complex (MACOM) consisting of WTAP, VIRMA, HAKAI, ZCH13H3, and RBM15/RBM15b (Figure 1A; Lence et al., 2019; Su et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: MACOM directly interacts with MAC to enhance m6A deposition.
source: MACOM directly interacts with MAC to enhance m6A deposition.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: In Arabidopsis thaliana, all subunits of both MAC and MACOM, except for RBM15/RBM15b, are conserved and play related roles in m6A deposition.
source: In Arabidopsis thaliana, all subunits of both MAC and MACOM, except for RBM15/RBM15b, are conserved and play related roles in m6A deposition, suggesting structural and topological conservation in plants (Růžička et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ime4 was strongly enriched in the Mum2 IP-MS analysis.
source: As expected, Ime4 was strongly enriched in the Mum2 IP-MS analysis.
evidence: This is supported by the IP-MS data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ygl036w and Kar4 were strongly enriched in the Mum2 IP-MS analysis.
source: We also identified two other proteins that were strongly enriched, Ygl036w and Kar4.
evidence: This is supported by the IP-MS data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pab1, Npl3, and Dyn2 were significantly enriched in the Mum2 IP, albeit to a lesser extent.
source: Two additional RNA-binding proteins, Pab1 and Npl3, and light chain dynein protein, Dyn2, were significantly enriched in the Mum2 IP, albeit to a lesser extent (log2 protein intensity fold change [FC] > 2, and -log t-test p-value>1).
evidence: This is supported by the IP-MS data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Slz1 was not significantly enriched in the Mum2 IP-MS analysis.
source: Noteworthy, Slz1, a known component of the MIS complex, was not significantly enriched (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the IP-MS data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mum2, Ime4, and Ygl036w significantly co-purified with Kar4 in Kar4 IP-MS.
source: Even though Kar4 enrichment was only fourfold over background, we found that Mum2, Ime4, and Ygl036w, but not Slz1, significantly co-purified with Kar4 (log2 protein intensity FC > 2, and -log t-test p-value>1).
evidence: This is supported by the IP-MS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Slz1 did not significantly co-purify with Kar4 in Kar4 IP-MS.
source: Even though Kar4 enrichment was only fourfold over background, we found that Mum2, Ime4, and Ygl036w, but not Slz1, significantly co-purified with Kar4 (log2 protein intensity FC > 2, and -log t-test p-value>1).
evidence: This is supported by the IP-MS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ime4, Ygl036w, Kar4, Slz1, and Dyn2 interact with Mum2 in an RNA-independent manner.
source: We conclude that Ime4, Ygl036w, Kar4, Slz1, and Dyn2 interact with Mum2 in an RNA-independent manner, while Pab1 interaction with Mum2 is RNA-dependent and hence indirect.
evidence: This is supported by RNase-treated IP-MS data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pab1 interaction with Mum2 is RNA-dependent and hence indirect.
source: We conclude that Ime4, Ygl036w, Kar4, Slz1, and Dyn2 interact with Mum2 in an RNA-independent manner, while Pab1 interaction with Mum2 is RNA-dependent and hence indirect.
evidence: This is supported by RNase-treated IP-MS data showing loss of Pab1 enrichment after RNase treatment (Figure 1C).

claim: mum2Δ cells showed a severe reduction in m6A over A levels.
source: Both deletion mutants showed a severe reduction in m6A over A levels as determined by LC-MS (Figure 1D), consistent with previous measurements (Ensinck et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: ime4Δ cells showed a severe reduction in m6A over A levels.
source: Both deletion mutants showed a severe reduction in m6A over A levels as determined by LC-MS (Figure 1D), consistent with previous measurements (Ensinck et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: slz1Δ cells showed a similar reduction in m6A levels as ime4Δ cells.
source: We found that slz1Δ cells showed a similar reduction in m6A levels as ime4Δ cells (LC-MS), suggesting that Slz1 is also required for m6A deposition (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Slz1 is required for m6A deposition.
source: We found that slz1Δ cells showed a similar reduction in m6A levels as ime4Δ cells (LC-MS), suggesting that Slz1 is also required for m6A deposition (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: m6A levels in slz1Δ cells did not accumulate at any time in the 12 hr following meiotic induction and showed background levels similar to ime4Δ cells.
source: However, m6A levels in slz1Δ cells did not accumulate at any time in the 12 hr following meiotic induction and showed background levels similar to ime4Δ cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by time-course LC-MS data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: kar4Δ cells showed no detectable m6A levels when entering meiosis.
source: We found that like ime4Δ cells entering meiosis, kar4Δ cells showed no detectable m6A levels (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: ygl036wΔ had no detectable m6A levels as determined by m6A-ELISA and m6A-seq2.
source: Both analyses by m6A-ELISA and m6A-seq2 showed that ygl036wΔ had no detectable m6A levels, similar to ime4Δ (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by m6A-ELISA and m6A-seq2 data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: dyn2Δ had reduced m6A levels (50% of WT) as detected by m6A ELISA.
source: Additionally, dyn2Δ had reduced m6A levels (50% of WT) as detected by m6A ELISA (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by m6A-ELISA data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Depletion of Pab1 and Npl3 showed no significant reduction in m6A levels compared to the control.
source: We found that depletion of Pab1 and Npl3 showed no significant reduction in m6A levels compared to the control (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by m6A-seq2 data after AID-mediated depletion shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Depletion of Slz1 showed a strong reduction in m6A.
source: As expected, depletion of Slz1 showed a strong reduction in m6A.
evidence: This is supported by m6A-seq2 data after AID-mediated depletion shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Pab1 and Npl3 are likely not part of the yeast MTC.
source: Also given that Pab1 and Npl3 interactions with Mum2 were RNA-dependent or not reproducible (in the case of Npl3), both RNA-binding proteins are likely not part of the yeast MTC.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-dependent interaction and lack of effect on m6A levels upon depletion.

claim: In addition to Ime4 and Mum2, Slz1, Kar4, and Ygl036w are all essential for m6A deposition.
source: We conclude that in addition to Ime4 and Mum2, Slz1, Kar4, and Ygl036w are all essential for m6A deposition.
evidence: This is supported by m6A quantification data from deletion mutants shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Ygl036w displayed a striking sequence similarity to VIRMA.
source: The analysis revealed that Ygl036w displayed a striking sequence similarity to VIRMA, a known subunit of the mammalian MTC.
evidence: This is supported by pairwise sequence comparison shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The top hit in proteome-wide structural alignment of Ygl036w against all predicted structures of the human proteome was VIRMA.
source: We next performed proteome-wide structural alignments of the predicted structure of Ygl036w against all predicted structures of the human proteome. The top hit in this analysis, by far, was VIRMA (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by structural alignment data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A structural alignment of Ygl036w against VIRMA displays a high extent of agreement (TM-score of 0.483, normalized for Ygl036w).
source: A structural alignment of Ygl036w against VIRMA displays a high extent of agreement (TM-score of 0.483, normalized for Ygl036w) (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by structural alignment data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Ygl036w and VIRMA are homologues.
source: These analyses thus strongly suggest that Ygl036w and VIRMA are homologues, and we hence renamed Ygl036W to Vir1, as the yeast orthologue of VIRMA in mammals, Virilizer in Drosophila, and VIR in plants, respectively.
evidence: This is inferred from sequence and structural similarity data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Slz1 showed partial similarity with ZC3H13.
source: Strikingly, Slz1 showed partial similarity with ZC3H13 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by pairwise sequence comparison shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Both SLZ1 and ZC3H13 have been proposed to play a similar role of shuttling the MTC complex into the nucleus.
source: Interestingly, both SLZ1 and ZC3H13 have been proposed to play a similar role, of shuttling the MTC complex into the nucleus (Schwartz et al., 2013; Wen et al., 2018), providing further evidence that these two proteins may be orthologues.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Five subunits of the mammalian MTC complex (METTL3, METTL14, WTAP, VIRMA, ZC3H13) likely have orthologues in the yeast counterpart (Ime4, Kar4, Mum2, Vir1, Slz1).
source: We conclude that the yeast MTC is considerably more conserved than previously described, with five subunits of the mammalian MTC complex (METTL3, METTL14, WTAP, VIRMA, ZC3H13) likely having orthologues in the yeast counterpart (Ime4, Kar4, Mum2, Vir1, Slz1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence and structural alignment data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Ime4, Mum2, and Vir1 are all required for mutual stabilisation in cells undergoing meiosis.
source: The analyses revealed that Ime4, Mum2, and Vir1 were all required for mutual stabilisation in cells undergoing meiosis, with protein levels of any of these three components being strongly reduced upon elimination of any of the other two (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of Ime4, Mum2, or Vir1 led to loss of Kar4.
source: Interestingly, loss of any of these proteins also led to loss of Kar4, yet – surprisingly – this was not mutual, as kar4Δ had little effect on the expression of any of the subunits (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: kar4Δ had little effect on the expression of Ime4, Mum2, or Vir1.
source: Interestingly, loss of any of these proteins also led to loss of Kar4, yet – surprisingly – this was not mutual, as kar4Δ had little effect on the expression of any of the subunits (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: slz1Δ had little effect on the expression of any of the MTC subunits.
source: The slz1Δ had little effect on the expression of any of the subunits (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of the different MTC components was not due to changes in RNA levels as shown by RNA-seq.
source: Importantly, loss of the different components was not due to changes in RNA levels as shown by RNA-seq as these remain relatively unchanged in the mutants except for Slz1, where SLZ1 mRNA induction was reduced in the deletion mutants resulting in lower Slz1 protein levels (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: In slz1Δ cells, the Mum2-Ime4-Vir1-Kar4 complex remained intact.
source: In line with the protein expression analysis of the m6A writer complex deletion mutants, we found that in slz1Δ cells the Mum2-Ime4-Vir1-Kar4 complex remained intact, and in kar4Δ cells Mum2 formed interactions with Vir1 and Ime4.
evidence: This is supported by Mum2 IP-MS data in slz1Δ cells shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In kar4Δ cells, Mum2 formed interactions with Vir1 and Ime4.
source: In line with the protein expression analysis of the m6A writer complex deletion mutants, we found that in slz1Δ cells the Mum2-Ime4-Vir1-Kar4 complex remained intact, and in kar4Δ cells Mum2 formed interactions with Vir1 and Ime4.
evidence: This is supported by Mum2 IP-MS data in kar4Δ cells shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Slz1 and Dyn2 were both enriched in the Mum2-IP in kar4Δ cells.
source: Slz1 and Dyn2 were also both enriched in the Mum2-IP in kar4Δ cells, suggesting that Kar4 does not mediate interactions between the other subunits of the m6A writer complex (Figure 4C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by Mum2 IP-MS data in kar4Δ cells shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Kar4 does not mediate interactions between the other subunits of the m6A writer complex.
source: Slz1 and Dyn2 were also both enriched in the Mum2-IP in kar4Δ cells, suggesting that Kar4 does not mediate interactions between the other subunits of the m6A writer complex (Figure 4C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the IP-MS data showing intact interactions in kar4Δ cells.

claim: Dyn2 was not identified as an interactor with Mum2 in the slz1Δ cells.
source: Interestingly, Dyn2 was not identified as an interactor with Mum2 in the slz1Δ cells, suggesting that Slz1 mediates the interaction of Dyn2 with the MTC (Figure 4C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by Mum2 IP-MS data in slz1Δ cells shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Slz1 mediates the interaction of Dyn2 with the MTC.
source: Interestingly, Dyn2 was not identified as an interactor with Mum2 in the slz1Δ cells, suggesting that Slz1 mediates the interaction of Dyn2 with the MTC (Figure 4C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of Dyn2 interaction in slz1Δ cells.

claim: Vir1, Mum2, Kar4, and Slz1 co-purified with Ime4 when co-expressed in insect cells.
source: The analyses revealed that Vir1, Mum2, Kar4, and Slz1 co-purified with Ime4 (Figure 4E), showing that these five subunits form a stable complex in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by SDS-PAGE analysis of purified recombinant complex shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The five subunits Ime4, Mum2, Kar4, Vir1, and Slz1 form a stable complex in vitro.
source: The analyses revealed that Vir1, Mum2, Kar4, and Slz1 co-purified with Ime4 (Figure 4E), showing that these five subunits form a stable complex in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by SDS-PAGE analysis of purified recombinant complex shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The yeast MTC comprises three mutually stabilizing components: (1) a core comprising Ime4, Mum2, and Vir1; (2) Kar4, which also is stabilized when part of the MTC; and (3) a module comprising Slz1 and Dyn2, where Slz1 acts as a hub for binding of Dyn2.
source: Collectively, these analyses suggest that the yeast MTC comprises three mutually stabilizing components: (1) a core comprising Ime4, Mum2, and Vir1; (2) Kar4, which also is stabilized when part of the MTC; and (3) a module comprising Slz1 and Dyn2, where Slz1 acts as a hub for binding of Dyn2.
evidence: This is inferred from the protein stability and interaction data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Ime4 has both m6A-dependent and m6A-independent functions in meiosis.
source: In yeast, Ime4 has both m6A-dependent and m6A-independent functions in meiosis as a catalytically inactive mutant of Ime4 shows milder delay in meiotic progression compared to the Ime4 deletion mutant (Agarwala et al., 2012; Clancy et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A catalytically inactive mutant of Ime4 shows milder delay in meiotic progression compared to the Ime4 deletion mutant.
source: In yeast, Ime4 has both m6A-dependent and m6A-independent functions in meiosis as a catalytically inactive mutant of Ime4 shows milder delay in meiotic progression compared to the Ime4 deletion mutant (Agarwala et al., 2012; Clancy et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and confirmed by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: IME4CD showed no m6A deposition and a milder delay in meiosis compared to the ime4Δ.
source: Indeed, we found that IME4CD showed no m6A deposition and a milder delay in meiosis compared to the ime4Δ (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by m6A quantification and meiotic progression data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: kar4Δ, vir1Δ, mum2Δ, and ime4Δ cells all displayed a strong defect in meiosis, with <40% completing meiotic divisions after 24 hr in SPO.
source: kar4Δ, vir1Δ, mum2Δ, and ime4Δ cells all displayed a strong defect in meiosis, and <40% completed meiotic divisions after 24 hr in SPO (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by DAPI counting data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: slz1Δ had a considerably milder phenotype in meiosis compared to ime4Δ cells.
source: In contrast, slz1Δ had a considerably milder phenotype in meiosis compared to ime4Δ cells (Figure 5A; Agarwala et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by DAPI counting data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: dyn2Δ showed the mildest phenotype in meiosis with only marginal delay in meiotic divisions and little effect on the number of cells that underwent meiosis after 24 hr in SPO.
source: dyn2Δ showed the mildest phenotype in meiosis with only marginal delay in meiotic divisions and little effect on the number of cells that underwent meiosis after 24 hr in SPO (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by DAPI counting data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: kar4Δ, vir1Δ, mum2Δ, and ime4Δ displayed the most severe expression phenotypes.
source: Consistent with the meiotic phenotypes, we found that kar4Δ, vir1Δ, mum2Δ, and ime4Δ displayed the most severe expression phenotypes (Figure 5C and D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C-D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Between the 4-to-6-hr time points, kar4Δ, vir1Δ, mum2Δ, and ime4Δ remained staggered at cluster C2, whereas WT transitioned into clusters C4 and C5.
source: This is most pronounced between the 4-to-6-hr time points, where kar4Δ, vir1Δ, mum2Δ, and ime4Δ remained staggered at cluster C2, whereas WT transitioned into clusters C4 and C5.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The different MTC mutants clustered together, suggesting a function common to all of them.
source: The fact that the different MTC mutants clustered together is highly suggestive of a function common to all of them, as opposed to moonlighting functions of individual components (Figure 5C and D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from PCA and clustering analysis shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: slz1Δ showed a mild delay, distinct from the remaining mutants.
source: Also consistent with the phenotypic analysis, slz1Δ showed a mild delay, distinct from the remaining mutants, whereas dyn2Δ showed little difference in comparison to WT (Figure 5C and D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: dyn2Δ showed little difference in comparison to WT in RNA-seq analysis.
source: Also consistent with the phenotypic analysis, slz1Δ showed a mild delay, distinct from the remaining mutants, whereas dyn2Δ showed little difference in comparison to WT (Figure 5C and D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: The histone genes HHF2 and HTB2 were significantly reduced in expression in five of the deletion mutants (ime4Δ, mum2Δ, slz1Δ, kar4Δ, vir1Δ) at the 2 hr time point.
source: Interestingly, despite the general lack of differences between the strains at the 2 hr time point, the histone genes, HHF2 and HTB2, were significantly reduced in expression in five of the deletion mutants (ime4Δ, mum2Δ, slz1Δ, kar4Δ, vir1Δ), potentially hinting at an early role of the MTC complex in regulation of histone levels, reminiscent of recent findings in planaria (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D; Dagan et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In WT cells, Pho92-bound transcripts were generally induced up to the 2 hr time point, following which their levels declined.
source: Using this subset of the transcripts, we observed that in WT cells these transcripts were generally induced up to the 2 hr time point, following which their levels declined.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis of Pho92-bound transcripts shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In all five deletion mutants essential for m6A (ime4Δ, mum2Δ, slz1Δ, kar4Δ, vir1Δ), Pho92-bound transcript levels failed to decline after their initial induction at 2 hr.
source: In contrast, in all five deletion mutants essential for m6A (ime4Δ, mum2Δ, slz1Δ, kar4Δ, vir1Δ), their levels failed to decline after their initial induction at 2 hr (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis of Pho92-bound transcripts shown in Figure 5E.

claim: dyn2Δ only showed marginal difference compared to the WT in Pho92-bound transcript levels.
source: Consistent with the m6A and meiotic phenotype, the dyn2Δ only showed marginal difference compared to the WT (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis of Pho92-bound transcripts shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Kar4, Mum2, Vir1, and Ime4 play a dual role in controlling the expression program of meiosis via both m6A-dependent and m6A-independent yet MTC-complex-dependent functions.
source: Taken together, these analyses suggest that Kar4, Mum2, Vir1, and Ime4 play a dual role in controlling the expression program of meiosis via both m6A-dependent and m6A-independent yet MTC-complex-dependent functions, in contrast to Slz1 exhibiting only an m6A-dependent function.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined phenotypic and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Slz1 exhibits only an m6A-dependent function.
source: Taken together, these analyses suggest that Kar4, Mum2, Vir1, and Ime4 play a dual role in controlling the expression program of meiosis via both m6A-dependent and m6A-independent yet MTC-complex-dependent functions, in contrast to Slz1 exhibiting only an m6A-dependent function.
evidence: This is inferred from the milder phenotype of slz1Δ compared to other MTC mutants.

claim: Kar4 is induced when haploid cells sense mating pheromone.
source: When haploid cells sense mating pheromone, Kar4 is induced and is recruited to promoters predominantly controlled by the transcription factor Ste12 to activate transcription of genes involved in the mating pathway (Gammie et al., 1999; Kurihara et al., 1996; Lahav et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Kar4 is recruited to promoters predominantly controlled by the transcription factor Ste12 to activate transcription of genes involved in the mating pathway.
source: When haploid cells sense mating pheromone, Kar4 is induced and is recruited to promoters predominantly controlled by the transcription factor Ste12 to activate transcription of genes involved in the mating pathway (Gammie et al., 1999; Kurihara et al., 1996; Lahav et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A shorter protein isoform of Kar4 was strongly induced when MATa cells were treated with mating pheromone (α-factor).
source: As expected, a shorter protein isoform of Kar4 was strongly induced when MATa cells were treated with mating pheromone (α-factor) (Figure 6A; Gammie et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Ime4 and Mum2 expression was not elevated upon pheromone treatment.
source: However, Ime4 and Mum2 expression was not elevated and Slz1 expression was not detected at all upon pheromone treatment.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Slz1 expression was not detected upon pheromone treatment.
source: However, Ime4 and Mum2 expression was not elevated and Slz1 expression was not detected at all upon pheromone treatment.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Kar4 levels were unaffected in ime4Δ and mum2Δ cells during mating.
source: We found that Kar4 levels were unaffected in ime4Δ, and mum2Δ cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Kar4 was bound to the AGA1 promoter upon mating pheromone treatment as determined by ChIP.
source: In line with protein expression data, we found that Kar4 was bound to the AGA1 promoter upon mating pheromone treatment as determined by ChIP, while other MTC subunits (Ime4, Mum2, Slz1) showed no enrichment (Figure 6C; Aymoz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Other MTC subunits (Ime4, Mum2, Slz1) showed no enrichment at the AGA1 promoter upon mating pheromone treatment.
source: In line with protein expression data, we found that Kar4 was bound to the AGA1 promoter upon mating pheromone treatment as determined by ChIP, while other MTC subunits (Ime4, Mum2, Slz1) showed no enrichment (Figure 6C; Aymoz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The yeast MTC does not play a role in the mating pathway.
source: These data indicate that the yeast MTC does not play a role in the mating pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of MTC component expression and chromatin binding during mating.

claim: Kar4-mNG concentrated inside the nucleus in MATa cells treated with α-factor.
source: We found that the Kar4 localization pattern was different between mating and meiosis. Kar4-mNG concentrated inside the nucleus in MATa cells treated with α-factor (Figure 6D and E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: During meiosis, Kar4-mNG was localized to both the cytoplasm and the nucleus.
source: During meiosis (MATa/α cells), however, we found that Kar4-mNG was localized to both the cytoplasm and the nucleus (Figure 6D and E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: Kar4 was bound to 800 genomic locations in MATa cells treated with α-factor.
source: While Kar4 was bound to 800 genomic locations in MATa cells treated with α-factor, only a few Kar4 peaks were detected during meiosis in MATa/α cells (<10) (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: Only a few Kar4 peaks were detected during meiosis in MATa/α cells (<10).
source: While Kar4 was bound to 800 genomic locations in MATa cells treated with α-factor, only a few Kar4 peaks were detected during meiosis in MATa/α cells (<10) (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: Kar4 ChIP-seq peaks were enriched for the Ste12-binding sites.
source: As expected, Kar4 ChIP-seq peaks were enriched for the Ste12-binding sites (motif 3 in Figure 6H), but other motifs were also identified, perhaps indicating that Kar4 can bind to promoters in a Ste12-independent manner (Figure 6H, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Kar4 can bind to promoters in a Ste12-independent manner.
source: As expected, Kar4 ChIP-seq peaks were enriched for the Ste12-binding sites (motif 3 in Figure 6H), but other motifs were also identified, perhaps indicating that Kar4 can bind to promoters in a Ste12-independent manner (Figure 6H, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is speculated based on the identification of other motifs in ChIP-seq data.

claim: ChIP-seq of Ime4, Mum2, and Slz1 showed no enrichment throughout the genome during meiosis.
source: In line with Kar4, ChIP-seq of Ime4, Mum2, and Slz1 showed no enrichment throughout the genome during meiosis (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ste12Δ did not affect the onset of meiosis.
source: We found that ste12Δ did not affect the onset of meiosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by DAPI counting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The Kar4 function in the MTC during meiosis differs from its known role as transcription regulator in the mating response pathway.
source: We conclude that the Kar4 function in the MTC during meiosis differs from its known role as transcription regulator in the mating response pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the different localization patterns and chromatin binding profiles of Kar4 during mating versus meiosis.

claim: Both Ime4 and Kar4 efficiently co-purify with mRNA following RNAse elution from oligo(dT) beads.
source: The assay revealed that both Ime4 and Kar4 efficiently co-purify with mRNA following RNAse elution from the beads, while pull-down from extracts pre-treated with RNAse did not show Ime4 and Kar4 signals with immunoblot as expected (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-protein interaction capture data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Kar4 can crosslink to RNA.
source: The analysis revealed Kar4 can crosslink to RNA (Figure 6I, Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by photo-activatable UV crosslinking data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Ime4 and Kar4 can both associate with mRNAs during early meiosis.
source: Thus, Ime4 and Kar4 can both associate with mRNAs during early meiosis.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-protein interaction capture and crosslinking data shown in Figure 6I and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Ime4 association with mRNAs is comparable in control and slz1Δ cells.
source: After the polyA pull-down, and elution with RNase, Ime4 was specifically enriched to comparable degrees in both the control and slz1Δ (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-protein interaction capture data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Ime4 association to mRNAs was reduced in kar4Δ cells.
source: In contrast, Ime4 association to mRNAs was reduced in kar4Δ cells with the no effect on Ime4 levels in input.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-protein interaction capture data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Kar4 is important for stabilizing the interaction between Ime4 (and likely the whole MTC) and mRNAs.
source: These data suggest that Kar4 is important for stabilizing the interaction between Ime4 (and likely the whole MTC) and mRNAs, and that Slz1 is not required for this.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced Ime4-mRNA association in kar4Δ cells.

claim: Slz1 is not required for stabilizing the interaction between Ime4 and mRNAs.
source: These data suggest that Kar4 is important for stabilizing the interaction between Ime4 (and likely the whole MTC) and mRNAs, and that Slz1 is not required for this.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparable Ime4-mRNA association in control and slz1Δ cells.

claim: The yeast MTC comprises six subunits of which five are essential for m6A deposition and have orthologues in the mammalian MTC.
source: Here, we showed that the yeast MTC comprises six subunits of which five are essential for m6A deposition and have orthologues in the mammalian MTC.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The yeast MTC is configured differently compared to the mammalian and Drosophila counterparts.
source: While the yeast MTC subunits are considerably more conserved than previously described, our findings suggest that the MTC is configured differently compared to the mammalian and Drosophila counterparts (see below).
evidence: This is inferred from protein interaction and stability data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The yeast MTC exerts both m6A-dependent and -independent functions that are both crucial for yeast meiosis.
source: The yeast MTC exerts both m6A-dependent and -independent functions that are both crucial for yeast meiosis.
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In yeast, the MAC and MACOM subunits are interweaved.
source: In yeast, we show that five subunits (Mum2, Ime4, Vir1, Kar4, and Slz1) are essential for m6A deposition and form a stable complex. We also provide evidence that the yeast MTC subunits Ime4, Mum2, and Vir1 stabilize each other and Kar4, indicating that in yeast the MAC and MACOM subunits are interweaved (Figure 7).
evidence: This is inferred from protein stability data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The interweaved arrangement of the yeast MTC is accompanied by loss of a mutual stabilizing interaction between Ime4 and Kar4.
source: This interweaved arrangement of the yeast MTC is accompanied also by loss of a mutual stabilizing interaction between Ime4 and Kar4, which is in contrast to their mammalian counterparts (Śledź and Jinek, 2016; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by protein stability data showing that kar4Δ does not affect Ime4 levels (Figure 4).

claim: Like its mammalian/Drosophila/plant counterparts, Vir1 has a central role in the MTC and m6A deposition.
source: Like its mammalian/Drosophila/plant counterparts, Vir1 has a central role in the MTC and m6A deposition.
evidence: This is supported by m6A quantification and protein stability data shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: Vir1 does not contain the VIRMA domain, which is thought to bridge the interaction between HAKAI and Fl2(d) in Drosophila.
source: Structurally, Vir1 and VIRMA showed strong conservation; however, Vir1 does not contain the VIRMA domain, which is thought to bridge the interaction between HAKAI and Fl2(d) in Drosophila (Bawankar et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The absence of the VIRMA domain in Vir1 may underlie the lack of a discernible HAKAI orthologue in yeast.
source: The absence of this domain may underlie the lack of a discernible HAKAI orthologue in yeast.
evidence: This is speculated based on the structural differences between Vir1 and VIRMA.

claim: In yeast, Vir1 stabilizes Mum2, Ime4, and Kar4, and is stabilized by Mum2 and Ime4.
source: We showed that in yeast Vir1 stabilizes Mum2, Ime4, and Kar4, and that it is stabilized by Mum2 and Ime4.
evidence: This is supported by protein stability data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the mammalian MTC, VIRMA and WTAP stabilize each other, but not METTL3 and METTL14.
source: This contrasts with the mammalian MTC, where VIRMA and WTAP stabilize each other, but not METTL3 and METTL14 (Yue et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Like METTL14, Kar4 is essential for m6A deposition and facilitates mRNA binding of the yeast MTC in vivo.
source: Like METTL14, Kar4 is essential for m6A deposition and facilitates mRNA binding of the yeast MTC in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by m6A quantification and RNA-protein interaction data shown in Figures 1 and 6.

claim: The role of Kar4 in bridging mRNA binding of the yeast MTC is critical since in yeast the MTC likely does not harbour a designed RNA binding protein such as RBM15.
source: We speculate that that the role of Kar4 in bridging mRNA binding of the yeast MTC is critical since in yeast the MTC likely does not harbour a designed RNA binding protein such as RBM15 (Patil et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculated based on the lack of an RBM15 orthologue in yeast.

claim: Slz1 is required for localizing the yeast MTC to the nucleus.
source: Previous work showed that Slz1 is required for localizing the yeast MTC to the nucleus, which is also consistent with findings for ZC3H13 in mammals where it also is important for MTC nuclear localization (Schwartz et al., 2013; Wen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ZC3H13 is important for MTC nuclear localization in mammals.
source: Previous work showed that Slz1 is required for localizing the yeast MTC to the nucleus, which is also consistent with findings for ZC3H13 in mammals where it also is important for MTC nuclear localization (Schwartz et al., 2013; Wen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In Drosophila, Flacc (ZC3H13/Slz1) bridges the interaction between Nito (RBM15) and the MTC.
source: In Drosophila, Flacc (ZC3H13/Slz1) bridges the interaction between Nito (RBM15) and the MTC (Knuckles et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Slz1 does not seem to be important for MTC association with mRNAs.
source: Slz1 does not seem to be important for MTC association with mRNAs and is dispensable for the m6A-independent role of the MTC.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-protein interaction data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Slz1 is dispensable for the m6A-independent role of the MTC.
source: Slz1 does not seem to be important for MTC association with mRNAs and is dispensable for the m6A-independent role of the MTC.
evidence: This is inferred from the milder phenotype of slz1Δ compared to other MTC mutants (Figure 5).

claim: Slz1 is essential for driving the m6A deposition reaction since cells lacking Slz1 showed no m6A.
source: However, Slz1 is essential for driving the m6A deposition reaction since cells lacking Slz1 showed no m6A.
evidence: This is supported by m6A quantification data shown in Figures 1D-E.

claim: ZC3H13 facilitates a conformational change in VIRMA and WTAP, which may be important for m6A deposition.
source: Recent structural work on the human MTC showed that ZC3H13 facilitates a conformational change in VIRMA and WTAP, which may be important for m6A deposition (Su et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Dyn2 is a subunit of the yeast MTC.
source: Our analysis showed that dynein light chain protein, Dyn2, is a subunit of the yeast MTC.
evidence: This is supported by IP-MS data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The interaction between Dyn2 and the yeast MTC Mum2 is RNA independent but requires Slz1.
source: Moreover, the interaction between Dyn2 and the yeast MTC Mum2 is RNA independent but requires Slz1.
evidence: This is supported by IP-MS data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Loss of Dyn2 led to a partial loss of mRNA methylation accompanied by a very mild meiotic phenotype.
source: In contrast to the remaining components, loss of Dyn2 led to a partial loss of mRNA methylation accompanied by a very mild meiotic phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by m6A quantification and meiotic progression data shown in Figures 2C and 5B.

claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans, a dynein light chain protein Dlc1 is involved in stabilizing the m6A writer Mett10.
source: However, it is worth noting that in Caenorhabditis elegans a dynein light chain protein Dlc1 is involved in stabilizing the m6A writer Mett10 (Dorsett and Schedl, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: m6A is deposited solely during early meiosis in yeast.
source: In yeast, m6A is deposited solely during early meiosis (Agarwala et al., 2012; Shah and Clancy, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: More than 1000 mRNAs are methylated during early yeast meiosis.
source: More than 1000 mRNAs are methylated during early yeast meiosis (Schwartz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Like in mammals, m6A-modified mRNAs are turned over more rapidly compared to unmodified mRNAs in yeast.
source: Like in mammals, m6A-modified mRNAs are turned over more rapidly compared to unmodified mRNAs (Bushkin et al., 2019; Scutenaire et al., 2022; Varier et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The decay of m6A transcripts requires active translation and is mediated by the YTH domain containing protein Pho92/Mrb1.
source: The decay of m6A transcripts requires active translation and is mediated by the YTH domain containing protein Pho92/Mrb1 (Varier et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Preventing the m6A modification at single meiotic transcripts can cause defects in meiosis.
source: Several studies have shown that preventing the m6A modification at single meiotic transcripts can cause defects in meiosis (Bushkin et al., 2019; Scutenaire et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.
